messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 55-year-old painter from Ghana who has been living in the United States for nearly thirty years, married to his wife, Akua, for twenty-five of them. The traumatic event that shattered his world happened two years ago, on a humid Tuesday evening in late August. His younger brother, Kofi, had just been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer, and Kwame had driven him home from the hospital. As they pulled into the driveway, Kofi suddenly clutched his chest, let out a soft gasp, and collapsed against the passenger seat. Kwame remembers the frantic call to 911, the way his hands shook as he tried to perform CPR, the sound of the ambulance sirens growing louder, and then the paramedics' faces as they finally shook their heads. Kofi died in Kwame's arms before the ambulance even arrived. That night, and for many nights after, Kwame could not close his eyes without seeing Kofi's face in that final moment—the slack jaw, the unseeing eyes. These visual memories would surge up unbidden, carrying with them a wave of grief so complete that it felt like his chest was caving in. Sometimes, even now, he will be standing at his easel, mixing paint, and suddenly the emotion hits him—the full, crushing weight of that loss—without any image at all. He will be flooded with a sorrow that has no picture, only a terrible, hollow ache.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found that certain things in his daily life became unbearable. The sound of an ambulance siren, even from blocks away, would stop him cold. His heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and his body would go rigid, as if bracing for another blow. He began to dread the evenings, because darkness reminded him of that drive home, and at night he found it harder to feel safe. His body stayed constantly tense, ready to react, even inside his own home—the place that had once been his sanctuary now felt like a stage where the memory could ambush him at any moment. At work, painting houses, he would sometimes hear a coworker mention a family member who had passed, and the casual comment would hit him like a physical shock. He would have to excuse himself, go to his truck, and sit with his head in his hands until the wave of grief and the images passed. These triggers—ambulances, the workplace, talk of loss—did not just bring the memory back; they also made Kwame feel, each time, that his life had been destroyed. He had come to believe that the man he was before Kofi died—the easygoing, confident painter who laughed easily and planned weekends with his wife—no longer existed. He felt isolated and set apart from others, as if he were living behind a pane of glass, watching the world go on without him. He did not know himself anymore, and this sense of identity loss made him feel more vulnerable, more on edge, because if he was not the person he used to be, then who was he, and what else might he lose?

This loop tightened over many months. The more Kwame felt that his life was destroyed, the more he noticed triggers everywhere. A conversation about loss would remind him of his own, and the memory would surge, and then the grief would reinforce his belief that he was permanently broken. He began to avoid his workplace altogether, taking only jobs where he worked alone, because he could not bear the risk of a coworker's casual remark. He stopped answering calls from his remaining siblings, because hearing their voices made the grief feel too fresh. He told Akua he was fine, but he knew she could see the tension in his shoulders, the way he flinched at unexpected sounds. He had stopped sleeping beside her, preferring the couch, because at night his mind would replay the ambulance ride, and he would feel his body go on alert again. The memory of Kofi's death made him feel more isolated, and the isolation made the memories more frequent. He was certain that if he let himself feel the full weight of it, he would never recover.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment at his daughter's school play. A child on stage delivered a line about losing a grandfather, and Kwame felt his chest tighten so severely that he had to leave the auditorium. He stood in the hallway, shaking, while the grief and the images and the sense that his life had been destroyed all crashed into him at once. Akua found him there, and for the first time, she did not look worried—she looked frightened. That night, she told him she could not watch him disappear anymore. Kwame is terrified that therapy will force him to relive that night in the driveway, but he is also terrified of what he has already become: a man who cannot paint, cannot sleep, cannot talk to his wife without feeling like a stranger in his own life. He wants to know if the man he used to be is still in there somewhere.
